extraction_notes.note: The elementary notation sentences for $Y \subseteq X$ and $x \in X$ at the start of Section 2 were not made definition nodes; the remarks after Lemma 4.1 ('We will alternate ...') and the acknowledgement were skipped as discussion.

Theorem 1.1 has no proof of its own: it follows from the sufficient conditions (7)-(9) stated in the introduction together with Section 6 (completeness of L_n) and Lemma 4.4; edges into TP1 record this, and the identification of L_n with the weak order of (O(V), sphere) is never stated explicitly.

The proofs of Theorems 5.2-5.4 use the existence of binary joins in L_{n-1} (the statement of Theorem 5.4 one dimension down) as induction hypothesis; adding Theorem 5.4 -> those proofs would create a result cycle, so the dependency is left implicit in their induction steps.

Section 6's argument that L_n is a complete lattice is in prose interleaved with Lemmas 6.1 and 6.2; the proof node runs from 'If $S$ is finite' to the end of Lemma 6.2's proof, with both lemmas nested in it as setup steps.
Several \ref's to Lemma 4.6 are written 'Theorem \ref{boundary}', and condition (7) writes $1_{a}$ for $1_G$; extracted verbatim.

nodes.name: signed group-set
nodes.statement: In \cite{Dyer} A signed group-set is defined to be a pair $(G,\Phi)$ satisfying the following conditions: \begin{enumerate}\item[(1)] $G$ is a group \item[(2)] $\Phi$ is a set with a given left action $(g,x)\mapsto gx$ by the product group $G\times \{\pm 1\}$. This action defines a pair of commuting left actions, by $G$ and $\{\pm 1\}$ on $\Phi$. \item[(3)] There is a specified partition $\Phi=\Phi^{+}\cup \Phi^{-}$ of $\Phi$ in to two disjoint subsets which are interchanged by the action of $-1$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I
differentia: There is a specified partition $\Phi=\Phi^{+}\cup \Phi^{-}$ of $\Phi$ in to two disjoint subsets which are interchanged by the action of $-1$.

nodes.name: root system and positive roots
nodes.statement: We call $\Phi$ the root system of $(G,\Phi)$ and $\Phi^{+}$ the set of positive roots.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I

nodes.name: inversion set $\Phi_g$
nodes.statement: For every $g\in G$, we define the subset $ \Phi_{g}:=\Phi^{+}\cap g(\Phi^{-})$. This is the set of positive roots which are made negative by $g^{-1}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I

nodes.name: weak order of a signed group-set
nodes.statement: The weak order of $(G,\Phi)$ is defined to be the set $\mathcal{L}:=\{\, \Phi_{g}\mid g\in G\,\}$ of subsets of $\Phi^{+}$, partially ordered by inclusion.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I
nodes.genus: the set $\mathcal{L}:=\{\, \Phi_{g}\mid g\in G\,\}$ of subsets of $\Phi^{+}$

nodes.name: Weak order of a Coxeter system as a signed group-set
nodes.statement: For a Coxeter system $(W,S)$, the usual standard root system $\Phi$ of $(W,S)$ together with a choice $\Phi^{+}$ of positive roots give rise to a signed group-set $(W,\Phi)$. The weak-order of this signed group set is exactly the usual weak order of $W$.
conclusions: the usual standard root system $\Phi$ of $(W,S)$ together with a choice $\Phi^{+}$ of positive roots give rise to a signed group-set $(W,\Phi)$.
The weak-order of this signed group set is exactly the usual weak order of $W$.

nodes.name: rootoidal signed group-set
nodes.statement: In \cite{Dyer}, $(G,S)$ is said to be rootoidal if the following additional conditions hold: \begin{enumerate}\item[(4)] If $g\in {G}$ with $\Phi_{g}=\emptyset$ then $g=1_{G}$. \item[(5)] $\mathcal{L}$ is a complete meet semilattice i.e. each of its non-empty subsets has a meet (greatest lower boind). \item[(6)] Given a non-empty family $(A_{i})_{i\in I}$ of $\mathcal{L}$ and $B\in \mathcal{L}$ such that $A_{i}\cap B=\emptyset$ for all $i\in I$, if the join (least upper bound) $A:=\bigvee_{i\in I} A_{i}$ exists in $\mathcal{L}$, then $A\cap B=\emptyset$. (This condition is called the JTP). \end{enumerate}
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I
differentia: $\mathcal{L}$ is a complete meet semilattice i.e. each of its non-empty subsets has a meet (greatest lower boind).
nodes.statement_short: Rootoidal: only the identity has empty inversion set, the weak order is a complete meet semilattice, and the join-trivial property (JTP) holds.

nodes.name: complete rootoidal signed group-set
nodes.statement: A particularly interesting class of rootoidal signed group-sets $(G,\Phi)$ are the complete ones: $(G,\Phi)$ is said to be complete if $\mathcal{L}$ has a maximum element, or equivalently if the weak order of $\mathcal{L}$ is a complete lattice.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I

nodes.name: rootoids and functor rootoids
nodes.statement: A (complete) signed groupoid-set gives rise to an associated (complete) rootoid, to which the extensive theory developed in \cite{Dyer} is applicable. For example, any homomorphism from a group (or groupoid) $H$ to $G$ gives rise to an associated ``functor rootoid'', which itself may be ``represented'' as a (complete) signed groupoid-set (the use of groupoid-sets rather than group-sets here is necessary in general even when $H$ and $G$ are both groups).
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I
nodes.statement_short: Complete signed groupoid-sets give complete rootoids; homomorphisms into $G$ yield functor rootoids represented as signed groupoid-sets.

nodes.name: orthogonal group $G=O(V)$ of a real Euclidean space
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a real Euclidean space and $G=O(V)$ be the orthogonal group of $V$.

nodes.name: root system $\Phi$ = unit sphere
nodes.statement: Let $\Phi$ be the unit sphere in $V$, with its natural action by $G\times\{\pm 1\}$.

nodes.name: positive roots from a total ordering
nodes.statement: Fix a vector-space total ordering $\preceq$ of $V$ and let $\Phi^{+}:=\{\, v\in \Phi\mid v>0\,\}$ and $\Phi^{-}:=-\Phi^{+}$.

nodes.name: The orthogonal group signed group-set is complete rootoidal
nodes.statement: The pair $(G,\Phi)$ defined above is a complete, rootoidal, signed group-set.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a real Euclidean space and $G=O(V)$ be the orthogonal group of $V$.
Let $\Phi$ be the unit sphere in $V$, with its natural action by $G\times\{\pm 1\}$.
conclusions: The pair $(G,\Phi)$ defined above is a complete, rootoidal, signed group-set.
nodes.statement_short: $(O(V),$ unit sphere$)$ with positive roots from a total order is a complete rootoidal signed group-set.

nodes.name: Sufficient conditions for complete rootoidal
nodes.statement: To prove the theorem, we shall use the fact that a signed group-set $(G,\Phi)$ with weak order $L$ is a complete rootoidal signed group-set if the following conditions hold: \begin{enumerate}\item[(7)] If $g\in {G}$ with $\Phi_{g}=\emptyset$ then $g=1_{a}$. \item[(8)] $L$ is a complete join semilattice i.e. each of subsets has a join \item[(9)] If $A\in \mathcal{L}$, then $\Phi^{+}\setminus A\in \mathcal{L}$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $L$ is a complete join semilattice i.e. each of subsets has a join
conclusions: a signed group-set $(G,\Phi)$ with weak order $L$ is a complete rootoidal signed group-set
nodes.statement_short: A signed group-set is complete rootoidal if only $1$ has empty $\Phi_g$, the weak order is a complete join semilattice, and it is closed under complement.

nodes.name: Proof of the sufficient conditions
nodes.statement: Indeed, (8) and (9) imply that $L$ is a complete meet semi-lattice by duality. To prove that the JTP holds, let $A_{i}$, $B$ be as in its statement. By (9), $A_{i}\subseteq \Phi^{+}\setminus B\in \mathcal{L}$ for all $i$, so by definition of join, $A=\bigvee A_{i}\subseteq \Phi^{+}\setminus B$ and $A\cap B=\emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: Duality gives meets from joins; complement closure (9) and the definition of join give the JTP.

nodes.name: set difference $X\backslash Y$
nodes.statement: If $X$ and $Y$ are sets with $Y \subseteq X$, we use $X\backslash Y$ to denote the set $\{x \in X | x \not\in Y\}$.

nodes.name: partially ordered set (poset)
nodes.statement: A partially ordered set or poset is a set $P$ equipped with a binary relation $\leq$ such that for all $x, y, $ and $z \in P$, \begin{enumerate} \item $x \leq x$, \item $x \leq y$ and $y \leq x$ imply $x = y$, \item $x \leq y$ and $y \leq z$ imply $x \leq z$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.genus: a set $P$ equipped with a binary relation $\leq$

nodes.name: totally ordered poset
nodes.statement: A poset $P$ with binary operation $\leq$ is totally ordered if given any pair of elements $\{x, y \} \in P$ we have either $x \leq y$ or $y \leq x$.

nodes.name: chain
nodes.statement: A poset $P$ is a {\bf chain} if for all $x, y \in P$, either $x \leq y$ or $y \leq x$.

nodes.name: order isomorphic posets
nodes.statement: Two posets $P$ and $Q$ are said to be {\bf order isomorphic} if there exists a map $\phi$ from $P$ onto $Q$ such that $x \leq y$ in $P$ if and only if $\phi(x) \leq \phi(y)$ in $Q$.

nodes.name: order isomorphism
nodes.statement: Such a map $\phi$ is called an order isomorphism from $P$ to $Q$.

nodes.name: dual poset
nodes.statement: Given a partially ordered set $P$ with order relation $\leq_{P}$, its dual, $P^{\delta}$, is the poset which is equal to $P$ as a set, with binary relation $\leq_{P^{\delta}}$ given by $x \leq_{P^{\delta}} y$ if and only if $y \leq_{P} x$.

nodes.name: upper bound
nodes.statement: Given a poset $P$ and a subset $S \subseteq P$, an element $x \in P$ is an {\bf upper bound} for $S$ if $y \leq x$ for all $y \in S$.

nodes.name: least upper bound
nodes.statement: An element $l \in P$ is a {\bf least upper bound} for $S$ if $l$ is an upper bound for $S$ and if $x$ is another upper bound for $S$, then $l \leq x$.

nodes.name: join notation $\bigvee S$
nodes.statement: The least upper bound of the set $S$ is denoted by $\bigvee S$ when it exists or $\bigvee_P S$ if it is unclear which poset we are considering.

nodes.name: binary join $x \vee y$
nodes.statement: In the case of two elements, we let $x \vee y$ denote the least upper bound of the two element set $\{x, y\}$.

nodes.name: lower bounds, greatest lower bounds, meets
nodes.statement: {\bf Lower bounds } and {\bf greatest lower bounds} are defined dually with $\bigwedge S$ denoting the greatest lower bound of the set $S$ and $x \wedge y$ denoting the greatest lower bound of the set $\{x, y\}$.

nodes.name: lattice and complete lattice
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a non-empty poset. If $x\wedge y$ and $x \vee y$ exist in $P$ for all $x, y \in P$, we say $P$ is a {\bf Lattice}. If $\bigwedge S$ and $\bigvee S$ exist in $P$ for every subset $S$ of $P$, then we say $P$ is a {\bf complete lattice}.

nodes.name: directed set
nodes.statement: If $S$ is a non-empty subset of a poset $P$, $S$ is said to be {\bf directed} if for every pair of elements $x, y \in S$, there exists $z \in S$, such that $z$ is an upper bound for the set $\{x, y\}$.
differentia: for every pair of elements $x, y \in S$, there exists $z \in S$, such that $z$ is an upper bound for the set $\{x, y\}$

nodes.name: Euclidean space $\Bbb{R}^{n+1}$ with standard basis
nodes.statement: We let $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ denote The Euclidean $(n + 1)$ space, with standard basis $\{e_1, e_2, \dots , e_{n + 1}\}$.

nodes.name: standard inner product $< , >$
nodes.statement: The standard inner product or dot product on $\Bbb{R}^{n+1}$ is denoted by $< , >$.

nodes.name: unit sphere $S^n$ and positive roots $\Phi_n^+$
nodes.statement: The unit sphere in $\Bbb{R}^{n+1}$ is $$S^n = \{(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n+1}) \in \Bbb{R}^{n+1} | x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \dots + x_{n+1}^2 = 1\}$$ and $\Phi_n^+$ is used to denote the set $$\Phi_n^+ = \{(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n + 1}) \in S^n | x_m = <x, e_m> > 0 \ \ \mbox{where} \ \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | x_i \not= 0\} \}.$$
nodes.statement_short: $S^n$ is the unit sphere; $\Phi_n^+$ is its points whose last nonzero coordinate is positive.

nodes.name: negative roots $\Phi_n^-$
nodes.statement: For its negative $ -\Phi_n^+ $, we use $$\Phi_n^- = \{(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n + 1}) \in S^n | x_m = <x, e_m> < 0 \ \ \mbox{where} \ \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | x_i \not= 0\} \}.$$

nodes.name: $S^n$ is the disjoint union of $\Phi_n^\pm$
nodes.statement: Note that $S^n = \Phi_n^+ \cup \Phi_n^-$ and $\Phi_n^+ \cap \Phi_n^-$ is empty.

nodes.name: orthogonal group $O(V)$
nodes.statement: For a Euclidean space $V$, we let $O(V)$ denote the orthogonal group of $V$.

nodes.name: orthogonal group $O_k$
nodes.statement: Sometimes we use $O_{k}$ to denote the orthogonal transformations of $\Bbb{R}^{k}$.

nodes.name: orthogonal maps preserve the inner product
nodes.statement: For any $T \in O_{n + 1}$, we have $<T(x), T(y)> = <x, y>$ for all $x, y \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$.

nodes.name: orthogonality $x\bot y$
nodes.statement: We write $x\bot y$ to denote that $<x, y> = 0$ for $x, y \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$.

nodes.name: orthogonal complement and orthogonal sum $V = V_1 \bot V_2$
nodes.statement: If $V_1$ and $V_2$ are subspaces of $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $V_1 + V_2 = V$ and $<v_1, v_2> = 0$ for all $v_1 \in V_1$ and $v_2 \in V_2$, then we say that $V_2$ is the orthogonal complement of $V_1$ in $V$ and we write the sum as $V = V_1 \bot V_2$.

nodes.name: orthogonal sum of transformations $T_1 \bot T_2$
nodes.statement: If $T_1 \in O(V_1)$ and $T_2 \in O(V_2)$ and $V = V_1 \bot V_2$, the linear transformation $T = T_1 \bot T_2$ is the unique linear transformation in $O(V)$ with the property that $T(v_1) = T_1(v_1)$ and $T(v_2) = T_2(v_2)$ for all $v_1 \in V_1$ and $v_2 \in V_2$.

nodes.name: identity maps $I_V$ and $1_{e_i}$
nodes.statement: We let $I_V$ denote the identity transformation on $V$ and we let $1_{e_i}$ denote the identity transformation on the subspace $\Bbb{R}e_i$ of $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$.

nodes.name: imbedding of $\Bbb{R}^k$ in $\Bbb{R}^{n+1}$
nodes.statement: We have a natural imbedding of $\Bbb{R}^{k}, k < n$ in $R^{n + 1}$ where we identify $\Bbb{R}^{k}$ with the set $\{(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n + 1} )| x_m = 0 \ \mbox{if} \ m > k \}$.

nodes.name: induced imbedding of $S^{k-1}$, $\Phi^\pm_{k-1}$
nodes.statement: This induces an imbedding of $S^{k - 1}, \Phi_{k - 1}^+$ and $\Phi_{k - 1}^-$ in $R^{n + 1}$.

nodes.name: topological closure $\bar{X}$
nodes.statement: The topological closure of a set $X \subseteq \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with respect to the metric defined by this norm on $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ is denoted by $\bar{X}$.

nodes.name: cone, convex cone, pointed convex cone
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product $<- , ->$. A subset $C \subseteq V$ is called a {\bf cone} if $C$ satisfies conditions (1) and (2) below: \begin{enumerate} \item $0 \in C$, \item If $v \in C$, then $\Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}v \subseteq C$. \noindent \leftline{C is called a {\bf convex cone} if it also satisfies the property:} \item If $u, v \in C$, then $u + v \in C$. \noindent A convex cone $C$ is a {\bf pointed convex cone} if it is a convex cone and satisfies the property: \item $C \cap (-C) = \{0\}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.origin_citation: Fenchel, Convex cones, sets, and functions
nodes.statement_short: A cone contains $0$ and is closed under nonnegative scaling; convex if closed under addition; pointed if $C\cap(-C)=\{0\}$.
nodes.label: cones

nodes.name: ray $(x)$
nodes.statement: Note that for any cone $C$ contained in $R^k$, $k > 0$, if $x \not= 0 \in C$, the {\bf ray} $(x) = \{rx | r \in \Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}\}$ is contained in $C$.

nodes.name: rays correspond to points of the sphere
nodes.statement: This ray intersects the unit sphere $S^{k - 1}$ at exactly one point $\frac{x}{||x||}$. Thus we have a one to one correspondence between the rays in $C$ and the points on the unit sphere $S^{k - 1}$ which are in $C$.

nodes.name: cone over a subset of the sphere $\widehat{X}$
nodes.statement: Let $X \subseteq S^n$, we use $\widehat{X}$ to denote the following cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$: $$\widehat{X} = \{rx | x \in X \ \mbox{and} \ r \in \Bbb{R}_{\geq 0} \} \ \mbox{if} \ X \not= \emptyset$$ and $\widehat{\emptyset} = \{0\}$.
nodes.label: hatconedef

nodes.name: cone-sphere correspondence
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be subsets of $S^n$. \begin{enumerate} \item $X = \widehat{X} \cap S^n$ and if $C$ is any cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = C\cap S^n$, then $\widehat{X} = C$, \item $X\cap Y = \emptyset$, if and only if $\widehat{X} \cap \widehat{Y} = \{0\}$. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: if $C$ is any cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = C\cap S^n$, then $\widehat{X} = C$
nodes.statement_short: $\widehat{X}$ is the unique cone meeting $S^n$ in $X$, and disjoint sets give cones meeting only in $0$.
nodes.label: hatcone

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement:
Assertion (1) is trivial if $X = \emptyset$, so let us assume for now that $X 
ot= \emptyset$. We have $\widehat{X}$ is a union of rays, $\widehat{X} =  igcup_{x \in X, x 
ot= 0} (x)$. Since each ray $(x)$ where $x \in X$ cuts the unit sphere exactly once at $x$, we have $X = \widehat{X} \cap S^n$. If C is a cone with $C \cap S^n = X$, then $\widehat{X} \subseteq C$, since the entire ray $(x)$ is in $C$ if $x \in X$. On the other hand, if $c \in C$, the ray $(c)$ cuts the sphere $S^n$ at $ rac{c}{||c||} \in X$. Therefore $( rac{c}{||c||}) = (c) \in \widehat{X}$ and since $C$ is the union of such rays, we have $C \subseteq \widehat{X}$. This proves (1). We can now relax the assumption that $X 
ot= \emptyset$. It is easily seen that $\widehat{X} \cap \widehat{Y} = \widehat{X \cap Y}$. Assertion (2) follows from the observation that if $C$ is a cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$, then $C \cap S^n = \emptyset$ if and only if $C = \{0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\widehat{X}$ as a union of rays, each meeting the sphere once; use $\widehat{X}\cap\widehat{Y}=\widehat{X\cap Y}$.

nodes.name: closure commutes with intersecting a convex cone with the sphere
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$, then $\overline{A \cap S^{n} } = \bar{A} \cap S^n$.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$
nodes.label: cone

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.4
nodes.statement: Let $A \subset \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ be a convex cone. Since $ \bar{A} \cap S^n$ is closed and contains $A \cap S^{n}$, we have $\overline{A \cap S^{n} } \subseteq \bar{A} \cap S^n$. On the other hand, if $x \in \bar{A} \cap S^n$, then $||x|| = 1$ and we have a sequence of points $\{x_i\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ in $A$ such that $\lim_{i \to \infty}x_i = x$. Since $A$ is convex we have the sequence of points $\{\frac{x_i}{||x_i||}\}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \in \bar{A} \cap S^n$. Given any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $m$ such that $| ||x_i|| - 1 | = | ||x_i|| - ||x|| | \leq ||x_i - x|| < \epsilon $ for all $i \geq m$. Since $$||x - \frac{x_i}{||x_i||}|| \leq ||x - x_i|| + ||x_i - \frac{x_i}{||x_i||}|| = ||x - x_i|| + \frac{||x_i||(| \ ||x_i|| - 1|)}{||x_i||} \leq 2\epsilon$$ for $i \geq m$, we have that the sequence $\{\frac{x_i}{||x_i||}\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ converges to $x$ and $x \in \overline{A \cap S^{n} }$.
nodes.statement_short: Easy inclusion by closedness; for the reverse, normalize an approximating sequence and estimate the distance.

nodes.name: closed half space, hyperplane, open half space
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product $<- , ->$. For any fixed $u \in V$, we let $H_u$ denote {\bf the closed half space} $H_u = \{v \in V | <v, u> \leq 0 \}$. We let $H(u)$ denote the {\bf hyperplane} $\{ v \in V | <v, u> = 0 \}$ and we let $H_u^{int}$ denote the {\bf open half space } $\{ v \in V | <v, u> < 0 \}$. \\ We will use the notation $H^V_u, H^V(u)$, and $H^{Vint}_u$ when we want to emphasize the underlying vector space.\\
nodes.origin_citation: Fenchel, Convex cones, sets, and functions
nodes.statement_short: $H_u=\{<v,u>\le 0\}$, $H(u)=\{<v,u>=0\}$, $H_u^{int}=\{<v,u><0\}$, with superscript $V$ for the ambient space.

nodes.name: half spaces determine their normals
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$. If $u, v \in V$ with $H(u) \subseteq H_v$, then $H(u) = H(v)$. Consequently if $u, v \in V$ with $H_u \subseteq H_v$, then $H_u = H_v$. Also $v_1 = \frac{-v}{||v||} \in H_v$ is the unique vector of norm one in $H_v$ with the property that $H_{v} = H_{-v_1}$.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$.
conclusions: Also $v_1 = \frac{-v}{||v||} \in H_v$ is the unique vector of norm one in $H_v$ with the property that $H_{v} = H_{-v_1}$.
nodes.statement_short: A hyperplane inside a half space is its boundary; nested half spaces are equal; the unit inward normal is unique.
nodes.label: hyper

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.6
nodes.statement: Suppose $u, v \in V$ with $H(u) \subseteq H_v = \{x \in V | <x, v> \leq 0 \}$. If $x \in H(u)$ with the property that $<x, v> \not= 0$, then $\{x,-x\} \in H(u)$ and either $<x, v> > 0$ or $<-x, v> > 0$ giving a contradiction. Hence $H(u) \subseteq H(v)$ and we have equality by comparing dimensions. If $H_u \subseteq H_v$, then $H(u) \subseteq H_v$ and therefore $H(u) = H(v)$. Now $V = <v> \bot H(v) = <u> \bot H(u) = <u> \bot H(v)$ and $u = cv$. Since $H_u \subseteq H_v$, $-u \in H_v$, hence $<-u, v> = <-cv, v> < 0$ and we have $c > 0$. Therefore $H_u = H_v$. Let $v_1 \in H_v$ such that $H_{-v_1} = H_{v}$, then as above, $-v_1 = cv$ for some $c > 0$. If we assume $||v_1|| = 1$, then we must have $v_1 = \frac{-v}{||v||} $.
nodes.statement_short: Antipodal points rule out $H(u)\not\subseteq H(v)$; compare dimensions and orthogonal decompositions to get $u=cv$, $c>0$.

nodes.name: open half spaces intersect
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$ and let $u, v \in V$. Then $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}$ is non-empty if $ u \not= -cv, \ c > 0$.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$ and let $u, v \in V$.
nodes.label: halfspaceintersect

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.7
nodes.statement: Let $u, v \in V$. Clearly $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int} = \emptyset$ if $u = -cv$ for some $c > 0$ in $\Bbb{R}$. Lets assume that $u \not= -cv, c > 0$. Suppose that $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int} = \emptyset$, then if $x \in H_u^{int}$ we must have $x \not\in H_v^{int}$ and $<x, v> \geq 0$ and $H_u^{int} \subseteq H_{-v}$. Taking closures, we get $H_u \subseteq H_{-v}$ and by Lemma \ref{hyper} $H_u = H_{-v}$ and $u = -cv$ for some $c > 0$ giving us a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: If the open half spaces were disjoint, taking closures gives $H_u\subseteq H_{-v}$, contradicting Lemma 3.6.

nodes.name: closure of intersection of open half spaces
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$ and let $u, v \in V$ for which $ u \not= -cv, \ c > 0$. Then $$\overline{H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}} = H_u \cap H_v.$$
assumptions: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$ and let $u, v \in V$ for which $ u \not= -cv, \ c > 0$.
nodes.label: closure

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.8
nodes.statement:
Let $u$ and $v$ be as in the statement of the lemma and let $C = H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}$. Clearly the lemma is true if $u = cv$ for some $c > 0$. Therefore we will assume that $u 
ot= cv$ for any $c \in \Bbb{R}$ for the rest of the proof. In this case $H(u) 
ot= H(v)$. Since $\overline{H_u^{int}} = H_u$ and $\overline{H_v^{int}} = H_v$, we have $C \subseteq H_{u} \cap H_{v}$ and since $H_{u} \cap H_{v}$ is a closed set, we have $ ar{C} \subseteq H_{u} \cap H_{v}$. To verify the opposite inclusion, consider $x \in H_{u} \cap H_v$. If $x \in C$, then $x \in  ar{C}$. Therefore we need only consider points $x$ where $<x, u> = 0$ or $<x, v> = 0$ or both. If $<x, u> = 0$ and $<x, v> > 0$, we have a sequence $\{x_i\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ in $H_{u}^{int}$ with $\lim_{i 	o \infty} x_i = x$. Now since $x \in H_{v}^{int}$ which is an open set, there exists an $m$ for which $x_i \in H_{v}^{int}$ for all $i \geq m$. Therefore $x_i \in C$ for all $i \geq m$ and $x \in  ar{C}$. A similar argument shows that if $<x, v> = 0$ and $<x, u> < 0$, we have $x \in  ar{C}$. Now if $<x, v> = 0$ and $<x, u> = 0$, then $x \in [H(u) \cap H(v)]$ which is a subspace of $H(v)$ of dimension $n - 2$ since $H(u) 
ot= H(v)$. Let $H = [H(u) \cap H(v)]$. It remains to show that $H \subseteq  ar{C}$. We consider $H$ as a hyperplane in $H(v)$. It is not difficult to see that if $y \in H(v)$, $<y, u> = < y, \pi(u)>$ where $\pi(u)$ is the orthogonal projection of $u$ onto the hyperplane $H(v)$. Therefore $$H = \{y \in H(v) | <y, \pi(u)> = 0 \} = H^{H(v)}(\pi(u))$$ as a hyperplane in $H(v)$. Now looking at the corresponding open half space in $H(v)$, we have $H_{\pi(u)}^{H(v){int}} = \{x \in H(v)| <x,\pi(u)> < 0\}$. By our reasoning above we know this is a subset of $ ar{C}$. Taking the closure within $H(v)$, we have $H^{H(v)}_{\pi(u)} = \overline{H_{\pi(u)}^{H(v)int} }\subseteq  ar{C}$ and $H = H^{H(v)}(\pi(u)) \subseteq  ar{C}$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Easy inclusion by closedness; reverse by cases on which defining inner products vanish, reducing the doubly-boundary case to a half space in $H(v)$.

nodes.name: maximal pointed convex cone
nodes.statement: A pointed convex cone $D$ in a Euclidean space $V$ is called {\bf maximal} if $D \cap (-D) = \{0\}$ and $D \cup (-D) = V$.
nodes.genus: A pointed convex cone $D$ in a Euclidean space $V$

nodes.name: maximal pointed convex cones define total orderings
nodes.statement: Note that a maximal pointed convex cone in a Euclidean space $V$ defines a total ordering on $V$ given by $y \leq x$ if and only if $y - x \in D$. Also $D = \{v \in V | v \leq 0\}$.

nodes.name: support of a cone
nodes.statement: A closed half space $H_u$ is called a {\bf support for a cone} $C$ if $C \subseteq H_u$.
nodes.origin_citation: Fenchel, Convex cones, sets, and functions

nodes.name: unique support of a maximal pointed convex cone
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in a Euclidean space $V$ with positive definite inner product $<-, - >$. Then $D$ has a unique support $H_v$, in $V$ and $H_v = \bar{D}$. Furthermore $H_v^{int} = \{x \in V | <x, v> < 0 \} \subset D$.
assumptions: Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in a Euclidean space $V$ with positive definite inner product $<-, - >$.
conclusions: $D$ has a unique support $H_v$, in $V$ and $H_v = \bar{D}$.
nodes.label: unique

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.11
nodes.statement: According to Corollary 1 to Theorem 1 of Fenchel \cite{Fenchel}, a maximal pointed convex cone $D$ in $V$, has a support $H_{v}$, where $D \subseteq H_{v}$. Now since $D \cup (-D) = V$ we have $H_v^{int} = \{x \in V | <x, v> < 0 \} \subseteq D$. Otherwise we would have $x \in (-D)$ with $<x, v> < 0$ and thus $<-x, v> > 0$ for $-x \in D$ giving us a contradiction. Thus we have $\overline{H_v^{int}} = H_{v} \subseteq \bar{D}$. On the other hand $\bar{D} \subseteq H_{v}$ since $D \subseteq H_{v}$, therefore $\bar{D} = H_v$. Suppose that $H_{u}$ is also a support. Then as above, we have $\bar{D} = H_u$ and hence $H_u = H_v$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a support from Fenchel's corollary; $D\cup(-D)=V$ forces the open half space into $D$, so $\bar{D}=H_v$, hence uniqueness.

nodes.name: maximal pointed convex cones correspond to ordered orthonormal bases
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a finite dimensional Euclidean space of dimension $n$ with positive definite inner product $< - , - >$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item D is a maximal pointed convex cone in V, \item There exists an ordered basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ of $V$ with $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_i \in \Bbb{R}, c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\},$$ \item There exists an ordered orthonormal basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ of $V$ with $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_i \in \Bbb{R}, c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ \end{enumerate} Moreover the map taking $D$ to $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ is a bijection from the maximal pointed convex cones in $V$ to the set of ordered orthonormal bases of $V$. The orthogonal group $O(V)$ acts simply transitively on the set of maximal pointed convex cones in $V$.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a finite dimensional Euclidean space of dimension $n$ with positive definite inner product $< - , - >$.
conclusions: Moreover the map taking $D$ to $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ is a bijection from the maximal pointed convex cones in $V$ to the set of ordered orthonormal bases of $V$.
The orthogonal group $O(V)$ acts simply transitively on the set of maximal pointed convex cones in $V$.

nodes.statement_short: A cone is maximal pointed convex iff it is the 'last nonzero coordinate negative' cone of an (orthonormal) ordered basis; $O(V)$ acts simply transitively on such cones.
nodes.label: equivalence

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.12
nodes.statement:
The result is obvious if $n = 1$, since the only maximal pointed convex cones of $\Bbb{R}e_1$ are $\Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}e_1$ and $\Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}(-e_1)$. We use induction on the dimension of $V$. Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$. From Theorem ef{unique} we know that $D$ has a unique support $H_{v_{n }}$, where $D \subseteq H_{v_{n }}$ and $H_{v_n}^{int} \subseteq D$. From Lemma ef{hyper} we know that we can choose a $v_n$ which is unique with the property that $-v_n \in D$, $||v_n|| = 1$ and $D \subseteq H_{v_{n }}$. Now consider the set $\widetilde{D} = D \cap H(v_{n })$. It is not difficult to see that $\widetilde{D}$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $H(v_{n })$. By induction, we get an orthonormal basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n - 1 }\}$ for $H(v_{n })$ such that $$\widetilde{D} = \{x \in H(v_{n }) | <x, v_m> < 0 \ \mbox{for} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | <x, v_m> 
ot= 0\}, 1\leq i \leq n -1 \} \cup \{0\}.$$ Now $D = \{x \in V | <x, v_{n }> < 0\} \cup \widetilde{D}$ and $$D = \{x \in V | <x, v_m> < 0 \ \mbox{for} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | <x, v_m> 
ot= 0\} , 1\leq i \leq n \} \cup \{0\}$$ where $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n\}$ is an orthonormal basis for $V$. This proves that (1) implies (3). That (3) implies (2) is trivial. To show that (2) implies (1), let $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ be an ordered basis of $V$ and let $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ It is trivial to check that $D$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$. Therefore (2) implies (1). Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$ with $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\} $$ where $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $V$. Suppose $\{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_n\}$ is another orthonormal basis of $V$ for which $$D = \{c_1u_1 + c_2u_2 + \dots + c_nu_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}. $$ We have both $H_{u_n}$ and $H_{v_n}$ are supporting half spaces for $D$. Therefore, by Theorem ef{unique} we have $H_{u_n} = H_{v_n}$ and since $||u_n|| = ||v_n|| = 1$, by Lemma ef{hyper}, $u_n = v_n$. Now $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1} \}$ and $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1} \}$ are ordered orthonormal bases of $H = H(u_n) = H(v_n)$ and $\widetilde{D} = D \cap H $ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $H$ with $$\widetilde{D} = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_{n- 1}v_{n-1} | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}$$ $$= \{c_1u_1 + c_2u_2 + \dots + c_{n- 1}u_{n-1} | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ Hence by induction, we have $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1} \}$ and $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1} \}$ are equal as ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and hence $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1}, u_n \}$ and\ $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1}, v_n \}$ are equal as ordered orthonormal bases of $V$. This shows that the map taking maximal pointed convex cones to ordered orthonormal bases given above is one to one. The map is onto since (3) implies (1). Since the orthogonal group $O(V)$ acts simply transitively on the set of ordered orthonormal bases of $V$, and by linearity the action commutes with the above map from ordered orthonormal bases to maximal pointed convex cones in $V$, we have a simple transitive action of $O(V)$ on the set of maximal pointed convex cones in $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $\dim V$: the unique support gives $v_n$, and $D\cap H(v_n)$ is maximal in $H(v_n)$. Uniqueness of the basis follows by applying the same reduction to two bases.

nodes.name: the poset $\mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: For $n \geq 0$ we let $\mathcal{L}_n$ denote the following poset of subsets of $S^n$ ordered by inclusion: $$\mathcal{L}_n = \{T(\Phi^-_n) \cap \Phi_n^+ | T\in O_{n + 1} \} .$$
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{L}_n$ is the set of $T(\Phi_n^-)\cap\Phi_n^+$, $T\in O_{n+1}$, ordered by inclusion.

nodes.name: $\Phi_n^+$ is the maximum of $\mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: Note that $\Phi_n^+ = T(\Phi^-_n)\cap \Phi_n^+$ when $T = -I_{\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}}$. This is a maximal element of $\mathcal{L}_n$.

nodes.name: cone $D_T$ of an orthogonal transformation
nodes.statement: If $T \in O_{n + 1}$ with $T(e_i) = v_i$, $1 \leq i \leq n + 1$, we let $$D_T = \{ v = \sum_{i = 1}^{n + 1}c_iv_i \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1} | <v, v_m> = c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where } \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0\}\} \cup \{0\}.$$

nodes.name: $D_T$ is a maximal pointed convex cone
nodes.statement: It is not difficult to show that $D_T $ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_T \cap S^{n} = T(\Phi_n^-)$.
conclusions: $D_T $ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_T \cap S^{n} = T(\Phi_n^-)$

nodes.name: unique maximal cone of an element of $\mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$, then there is a unique maximal pointed convex cone $D_X = D_{T_X}$ in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with the property that $X = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+$.
conclusions: there is a unique maximal pointed convex cone $D_X = D_{T_X}$ in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with the property that $X = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+$.
nodes.label: mpcc

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement: From its definition, we have that $D_{T_X}$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_{T_X} \cap \Phi_n^+ = T_X(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+ = X$. Suppose that $D$ is another maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = D \cap \Phi_n^+$. If $D_e = D_{-I_{\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}}}$, then $\Phi_n^+ = D_e \cap S^n$ and $X = D_X \cap D_e \cap S^n = D \cap D_e \cap S^n$. Now $C_1 = D_X \cap D_e$ and $C_2 = D \cap D_e$ are both convex cones in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = C_1 \cap S^n = C_2 \cap S^n$. By Lemma \ref{hatcone}, $\hat{X} = C_1 = C_2$. Let $C'_1 = (D_e \backslash C_1) \cup \{0\} = D_e \cap (-D_X)$. Now $$[C_1 \cup (-C'_1) ] \cup [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = D_e \cup (-D_e) = \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$$ and $$[C_1 \cup (-C'_1) ] \cap [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = \{0\}$$ since $C_1 \cup (-C'_1) \subseteq D_X$ and $C'_1 \cup (-C_1) \subseteq -D_X$. Since $D_X \cap [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = \{0\}$, we can conclude that $D_X = C_1 \cup (-C'_1)$. Since $C'_1 = (D_e \backslash C_2) \cup \{0\} = D_e \cap (-D)$, we can similarly conclude that $D = C_1 \cup (-C'_1)$ and hence $D = D_X$.
nodes.statement_short: Existence from $D_{T_X}$; uniqueness by decomposing any such cone as $C_1\cup(-C_1')$ with $C_1=\widehat{X}$ fixed by Lemma 3.3.

nodes.name: cones $D_e$ and $D_X$
nodes.statement: We define $D_e = D_{-I_{\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}}}$, that is $$D_e = \{ x = \sum_{i = 1}^{n + 1}c_ie_i \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1} | <x, e_m> = c_m > 0 \ \mbox{where } \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0\}\} \cup \{0\}$$ and $D_e \cap S^n = \Phi_n^+$. For $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$ we let $D_X$ denote the unique maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ for which $X = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+ = D_X \cap D_e \cap S^n$.
nodes.label: mpccX

nodes.name: characterization of $\mathcal{L}_n$ by maximal cones
nodes.statement: Therefore we can characterize $\mathcal{L}_n$ as $$\mathcal{L}_n = \{D\cap \Phi_n^+ | D \ \mbox{is a maximal pointed convex cone in } \ \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}\}.$$
conclusions: $$\mathcal{L}_n = \{D\cap \Phi_n^+ | D \ \mbox{is a maximal pointed convex cone in } \ \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}\}.$$

nodes.name: $\mathcal{L}_0$
nodes.statement: If $n = 0$, then $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1} = \Bbb{R}^1 = \Bbb{R}e_1$. We have $S^0 = \{-e_1, e_1\}, \Phi_0^+ = \{e_1\}$ and $O_1 = \{\pm 1_{e_1}\}$. Therefore $\mathcal{L}_0 = \{\emptyset, \{e_1\}\}$.

nodes.name: complementation duality of $\mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, then $\Phi^+_n \backslash X$ is also an element of $\mathcal{L}_n$. The map $\phi: \mathcal{L}_n \to \mathcal{L}_n^{\delta}$ given by $\phi(X) = \Phi^+_n \backslash X$ is an order isomorphism of posets.
conclusions: $\Phi^+_n \backslash X$ is also an element of $\mathcal{L}_n$.
The map $\phi: \mathcal{L}_n \to \mathcal{L}_n^{\delta}$ given by $\phi(X) = \Phi^+_n \backslash X$ is an order isomorphism of posets.
nodes.label: duality

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.4
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$. There exists a maximal pointed convex cone $D$ in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ for which $X = D \cap \Phi_n^+$. We have that $(-D)$ is also a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ and $(-D)\cap \Phi_n^+ = \Phi_n^+ \backslash X$. Hence $\Phi_n^+ \backslash X \in \mathcal{L}_n$. Since $\phi^2(X) = X$, it is easy to see that $\phi$ is a bijective map. Since $ \Phi_n^+ \backslash X \subseteq \Phi_n^+ \backslash Y$ if and only if $X \supseteq Y$, we have an isomorphism of posets $\phi: \mathcal{L}_n \to \mathcal{L}_n^{\delta}$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace the cone $D$ by $-D$; complementation is an involution reversing inclusion.

nodes.name: restriction of $\mathcal{L}_n$ to $\Bbb{R}^n$
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an element of $\mathcal{L}_n$, then $X \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }$ is an element of $\mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$, where $\Bbb{R}^n $ is imbedded in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1} $ as in Section \ref{intro}.
assumptions: where $\Bbb{R}^n $ is imbedded in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1} $ as in Section \ref{intro}.
nodes.label: projection

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.5
nodes.statement: Given $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, we have a maximal pointed convex cone $D \subset \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ such that $X = D \cap \Phi_n^+$. Let $\widetilde{D} = D \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }$. It is not difficult to see that $\widetilde{D}$ is a maximal pointed convex cone of $\Bbb{R}^{n }$ and therefore $X \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } = D \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+ = \widetilde{D} \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+ \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Intersect the maximal cone $D$ with $\Bbb{R}^n$, which is again maximal pointed convex.

nodes.name: boundary description of $\bar{X}$
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $X = T_X(\Phi^-_n)\cap \Phi^+_n$ for some $T_X \in O_{n + 1}$. Let $u_X = T_X(e_{n + 1})$ and $e = -e_{n + 1}$. If $u_X \not= e_{n + 1} = -e$, then \begin{enumerate} \item $X = (X\cap H(u_X)) \cup \{x \in \Phi_n^+ | <x, u_X> < 0 \},$ \item $\bar{X} = [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}] \cap S^n$, \item $\bar{X} \cap S^{n -1} = H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1} \supseteq H(u_X)\cap S^{n - 1}$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $X = T_X(\Phi^-_n)\cap \Phi^+_n$ for some $T_X \in O_{n + 1}$.
nodes.statement_short: For $X\in\mathcal{L}_n$ with $u_X\ne e_{n+1}$, $\bar{X}$ is the intersection of two closed half spaces with $S^n$.
nodes.label: boundary

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.6
nodes.statement: (1) follows from the fact that $X = T_X(\Phi^-_n) \cap \Phi^+_n$ and that $$ T_X(\Phi_n^-) = \{x \in S^n| x = \sum_{i = 1}^{n + 1}c_iT_X(e_i) \ \mbox{such that } \ c_m < 0 , \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i| c_i \not= 0\}\}.$$ Assertion (3) follows from (2) since, given (2), we have $$\bar{X}\cap S^{n -1} = [H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1}] \cap [H_{e} \cap S^{n - 1}] \cap [S^n \cap S^{n - 1}] = [H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1}] \cap S^{n - 1}.$$ It remains to prove (2). Let $C$ be the convex cone $[H_{u_X}^{int} \cap H_{e}^{int}] \cup \{0\}$, the intersection of the two open half spaces with the zero vector attached. $C$ is non-empty by Lemma \ref{halfspaceintersect}. Now $C \cap S^{n} \subset X \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n $ and hence $$ \overline{C \cap S^{n} } \subseteq \overline{X} \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n .$$ By Lemma \ref{cone} $$\overline{C} \cap S^{n} \subseteq \overline{X} \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n. $$ By Lemma \ref{closure}, $\bar{C} = H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}$. Therefore $\overline{X} = [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n$ and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: (1) from the description of $T_X(\Phi_n^-)$, (3) from (2); (2) by sandwiching $\bar{X}$ between closures of open and closed half-space cones (Lemmas 3.4, 3.7, 3.8).

nodes.name: equality of hyperplane traces
nodes.statement: Let $X$, $Y \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = T_Y(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$. Let $u_X = T_X(e_{n + 1})$ and let $u_Y = T_Y(e_{n + 1})$. If $H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \not= \Bbb{R}^{n }$ and $H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \subseteq H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }$, then $$H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } = H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }.$$
nodes.label: equality

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.7
nodes.statement: We have $ H(u_Y)\cap \Bbb{R}^{n } $ is a subspace of $\Bbb{R}^{n}$ of dimension $n$ or of dimension $n - 1$ . Since we are assuming that $H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \not= \Bbb{R}^{n }$, it must be a subspace of dimension $n - 1$. Since $H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^n \subseteq H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^n$ it too must be a subspace of dimension $n - 1$ and hence must be all of $H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Dimension count: both traces are $(n-1)$-dimensional subspaces, one inside the other.

nodes.name: transformations fixing $\Bbb{R}^n$
nodes.statement: Let $Z \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $Z = T_Z(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+$ for some $T_Z \in O_{n + 1}$. Let $u_Z = T_Z(e_{n + 1})$. If $H(u_Z) = \Bbb{R}^n$, then $T_Z = T'_Z \bot \pm 1_{e_{n + 1}}$ for some $T'_Z \in O_n$.
assumptions: Let $Z \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $Z = T_Z(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+$ for some $T_Z \in O_{n + 1}$.
nodes.label: Z

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.8
nodes.statement: Since $T_Z$ is an isometry, with $T_Z(\Bbb{R}^n) = H(u_Z) = \Bbb{R}^n$, we have $T_Z|_{\Bbb{R}^n} = T'_Z \in O_n$. Now $||u_Z|| = 1$ and $<u_Z, x> = 0$ for all $x \in \Bbb{R}^n$. Hence $u_Z = \pm e_{n + 1}$ and $T_Z = T'_Z\bot \pm 1_{e_{n + 1}}$.
nodes.statement_short: $T_Z$ preserves $\Bbb{R}^n$, so $u_Z$ is a unit normal to $\Bbb{R}^n$, i.e. $\pm e_{n+1}$.

nodes.name: joins exist in $\mathcal{L}_0$
nodes.statement: Obviously we can find $X\vee Y$ in $\mathcal{L}_0$ for any pair of elements $\{X, Y\}$ in $\mathcal{L}_0$.
nodes.section: 5 The least upper bound of two elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$.
conclusions: we can find $X\vee Y$ in $\mathcal{L}_0$ for any pair of elements $\{X, Y\}$ in $\mathcal{L}_0$

nodes.statement:
Let $X, Y \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = T_Y(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$, where $T_X, T_Y \in O_{n + 1}$. Let $u_X = T_X(e_{n + 1})$ and $u_Y = T_Y(e_{n + 1})$. Assume that $H(u_X) 
ot= \Bbb{R}^{n}$ and $H(u_Y) 
ot= \Bbb{R}^{n}$. Then if $H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.2
nodes.statement: Let $X_1 = X \cap \Bbb{R}^n$ and $Y_1 = Y \cap \Bbb{R}^n$. Then by Theorem \ref{projection} we have $X_1 \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1} $ and $Y_1 \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$. We proceed by induction. Let $Z_1 \in \mathcal{L}_{n -1}$ where $Z_1$ is the least upper bound of $\{X_1, Y_1\} $ in $ \mathcal{L}_{n -1}$. Then $Z_1 = D_{Z_1} \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+$ for a unique maximal pointed convex cone of $\Bbb{R}^n$. Let $D_Z = D_{Z_1} \cup \{x \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1} | <x, e_{n + 1}> > 0\}$. It is not difficult to see that $D_Z$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_Z \cap \Bbb{R}^n = D_{Z_1}$. We let $Z = D_Z \cap \Phi_n^+ \in \mathcal{L}_n$. Then $Z\cap S^{n - 1} = Z_1$ and therefore $$X = X_1 \cup [X \cap \{x \in S^n | <x, e_{n + 1}> > 0\}] \subseteq Z$$ and $$Y = Y_1 \cup [Y \cap \{x \in S^n | <x, e_{n + 1}> > 0\}] \subseteq Z.$$ Now, if $W \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with the property that both $X$ and $Y$ are subsets of $W$, then Theorem \ref{conditions} tells us that $\{x \in S^n | <x, e_{n + 1}> > 0\} \subseteq W$. Since $W\cap S^{n - 1}$ contains both $X_1$ and $Y_1$ and, according to Theorem \ref{projection}, $W\cap S^{n - 1} \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$, we must have $Z_1 = Z\cap S^{n - 1} \subset W\cap S^{n - 1} \subseteq W$. Therefore $Z \subseteq W$ and $Z$ is the least upper bound of $\{X, Y\}$ in $\mathcal{L}_n$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.3
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be as in the statement of the theorem with $\bar{X} \subseteq \bar{Y}$. Then $X = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+$ where $D_X$ and $D_Y$ are maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$. Suppose $Z = T_Z(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+ = D_Z\cap \Phi_n^+ \in \mathcal{L}_n$ is an upper bound for $\{X, Y\}$, where $T_Z \in O_{n + 1}$ and $D_Z$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$. Now $Z = X \vee Y$ if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are contained in $Z$ and if $D_1$ is any maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ for which $X$ and $Y$ are contained in $D_1 \cap \Phi^+_n$, then $Z = D_Z \cap \Phi^+_n \subseteq D_1 \cap \Phi^+_n$. We will use this characterization of $X\vee Y$ and induction on $n$ to show that $Z = X\vee Y$ exists in $\mathcal{L}_n$. We have already noted that we can find the join of any two elements in $\mathcal{L}_0$. Let $u_Y = T_Y(e_{n + 1})$ and recall the definition of $D_e$ from Definition \ref{mpccX}. We first work on constructing that part of the boundary of $Z$ which meets $H(u_Y)$. Let $$\dddot{\Phi} = \Phi_n^+ \cap H(u_Y) = D_e \cap H(u_y) \cap S^{n} = \dddot{D_e}\cap S^{n },$$ where $\dddot{D_e} = D_e \cap H(u_y)$. We let $$\dddot{X} = X \cap H(u_Y) = D_X \cap H(u_Y) \cap \Phi_n^+ = \dddot{D_X} \cap \Phi_n^+ = \dddot{D_X} \cap \dddot{\Phi}$$ where $\dddot{D_X} = D_X \cap H(u_Y)$ and let $$\dddot{Y} = Y \cap H(u_Y) =D_Y \cap H(u_Y) \cap \Phi_n^+ = \dddot{D_Y} \cap \Phi_n^+ = \dddot{D_Y} \cap \dddot{\Phi}$$ where $\dddot{D_Y} = D_Y \cap H(u_Y)$. Now $\dddot{D}_X$, $\dddot{D}_Y $ and $\dddot{D_e}$ are maximal pointed convex cones of $H(u_Y)$. Therefore $T_Y^{-1}(\dddot{D_e})$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^n$. Now by Theorem \ref{equivalence} There exists an ordered orthonormal basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ of $\Bbb{R}^n$ with $$T_Y^{-1}(\dddot{D_e}) = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ Let $T_1$ be the orthogonal transformation in $O_n$ that sends $e_i$ to $-v_i$, $1 \leq i \leq n$. Then $$T_1^{-1}(T_Y^{-1}(\dddot{\Phi})) = T_1^{-1}(T_Y^{-1}(\dddot{D_e}\cap S^{n })) = T_1^{-1}(T_Y^{-1}(\dddot{D_e}))\cap T_1^{-1}(T_Y^{-1}(S^{n })) = \Phi^+_{n - 1}.$$ Letting $T :H(u_Y) \to \Bbb{R}^n$ denote the isometry $T = T_1^{-1}T_Y^{-1} $, we get $T(\dddot{\Phi}) = \Phi^+_{n - 1}$ and $$ \widetilde{X} = T(\dddot{X}) = T(\dddot{D_X}) \cap T(\dddot{\Phi}) = T(\dddot{D_X}) \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+ \in \mathcal{L}_{n -1}. $$ since $T(\dddot{D_X})$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^n$. Similarly $\widetilde{Y} = T(\dddot{Y}) \in \mathcal{L}_{n -1}$. Using our inductive assumption, we can find $\widetilde{Z} \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$ with $\widetilde{Z} = \widetilde{X}\vee \widetilde{Y}$. Now $\widetilde{Z} = D_{\widetilde{Z}} \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+$ for some maximal pointed convex cone $D_{\widetilde{Z}}$ in $\Bbb{R}^n$ and if $D$ is another maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^n$ for which $ D \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+$ is an upper bound for $\{\widetilde{X}, \widetilde{Y}\}$, then $ D_{\widetilde{Z}} \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+ \subseteq D \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+$. The isometry $T^{-1} : \Bbb{R}^n \to H(u_Y)$ gives a bijection between maximal pointed convex cones in $\Bbb{R}^n$ and maximal pointed convex cones in $H(u_Y)$. Therefore $$\dddot{Z} = T^{-1}(\widetilde{Z}) = T^{-1}(D_{\widetilde{Z}}) \cap T^{-1}(\Phi_{n - 1}^+) = T^{-1}(D_{\widetilde{Z}}) \cap \dddot{\Phi}$$ contains $\dddot{X}$ and $\dddot{Y}$ and if $D_1$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $H(u_Y)$ for which $D_1 \cap \dddot{\Phi}$ contains $\dddot{X}$ and $\dddot{Y}$, then $\dddot{Z} \subseteq D_1 \cap \dddot{\Phi}$. We let $\dddot{D_Z} = T^{-1}(D_{\widetilde{Z}})$, a maximal pointed convex cone in $H(u_Y)$ with $\dddot{D_Z} \cap \dddot{\Phi} = \dddot{Z}$ . Consider $H_{u_Y}^{int} = \{x \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1} | <x, u_Y> < 0 \}$. We have $Y = \dddot{Y} \cup (H_{u_Y}^{int} \cap \Phi_{n}^+$). Now $$X = \dddot{X} \cup \{x \in X | <x, u_Y> < 0\} = \dddot{X} \cup [X \cap (H_{u_Y}^{int} \cap \Phi_{n}^+)]$$ since $\bar{X} \subseteq \bar{Y} \subseteq H_{u_Y}$. Let $D_Z = \dddot{D_{Z}} \cup H_{u_Y}^{int}$. It is clear that $D_Z$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_Z \cap H(u_Y) = \dddot{D_Z}$. I claim that $Z = D_Z \cap \Phi^+_n$ is the least upper bound of $\{X, Y\}$ in $\mathcal{L}_n$. Certainly $$X\subseteq \dddot{X} \cup [ H^{int}_{u_Y} \cap \Phi^+_n] \subseteq \dddot{Z} \cup [ H^{int}_{u_Y} \cap \Phi^+_n] \subseteq Z$$ and similarly $Y \subseteq Z$. Now suppose $D'$ is another maximal pointed convex cone of $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with the property that $D' \cap \Phi_n^+$ contains both $X$ and $Y$. We must show that $Z \subseteq D' \cap \Phi_n^+$. We have $\dddot{X} \subseteq X \subseteq D' \cap \Phi_n^+$ and $\dddot{Y} \subseteq Y \subseteq D' \cap \Phi_n^+$. If we let $\dddot{D'} = D' \cap H(u_Y)$, then $\dddot{D'} $ is a maximal pointed cone of $H(u_Y)$ and $\dddot{D'} \cap \dddot{\Phi}$ contains both $\dddot{X}$ and $\dddot{Y}$. Therefore as shown above, $\dddot{Z} = \dddot{D_{Z}} \cap \dddot{\Phi} \subseteq \dddot{D'} \cap \dddot{\Phi} \subseteq D' \cap \Phi_n^+$. Now since $(H_{u_Y}^{int} \cap \Phi_{n}^+) \subseteq Y \subseteq D' \cap \Phi_n^+$, we have that $Z = (\dddot{D_{Z}} \cap\dddot{\Phi}) \cup (H_{u_Y}^{int} \cap \Phi_{n}^+) \subseteq D' \cap \Phi_n^+$. This completes that proof that $Z = X\vee Y$ in $\mathcal{L}_n$.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{L}_n$ is a complete lattice
nodes.statement: In this section, we show that $\mathcal{L}_{n }$ is a complete lattice, that is given any subset $S$ of $\mathcal{L}_{n }$, $\bigwedge S$ and $\bigvee S$ exist in $\mathcal{L}_{n }$.
conclusions: $\mathcal{L}_{n }$ is a complete lattice, that is given any subset $S$ of $\mathcal{L}_{n }$, $\bigwedge S$ and $\bigvee S$ exist in $\mathcal{L}_{n }$.

nodes.name: Proof that $\mathcal{L}_n$ is a complete lattice
nodes.statement:
If $S$ is finite, we already have that $ igvee S$ exists in $\mathcal{L}_{n }$, by induction and $ igwedge S$ exists by duality. The full result will follow from exercise 7.5 in \cite{DnP} when we have shown that the result is true for directed sets.  egin{lemma} {( Exercise 7.5 \cite{DnP})} Let $P$ be an ordered set such that the join of any two elements in $P$ exists in $P$. Let $S \subseteq P$ Let $D$ be the directed set $D = \{ igvee F | \emptyset 
ot= F \subseteq S, F \ \mbox{finite} \}$. Then $ igvee S =  igvee D$ if $ igvee D$ exists. \end{lemma}  egin{proof} If $U$ is an upper bound for $S,$ then $U$ is an upper bound for any finite subset $F$ of $S$ and hence $ igvee F \leq U$. Therefore $D_1 \leq U$ for all $D_1 \in D$ and $ igvee D \leq  igvee S$ if they exist. On the other hand, given any $s \in S$, we have $s = s \vee s \in D$ and $s \leq  igvee D$ if $ igvee D$ exists. Therefore $ igvee D$ is an upper bound for $S$ and $ igvee S \leq  igvee D$. \end{proof} In order to show that $\mathcal{L}_{n }$ is a complete lattice, it remains to show that any directed set in $\mathcal{L}_{n }$ has a least upper bound. It will then follow from the above Lemma that every subset $S$ of $\mathcal{L}_{n }$ has a least upper bound and the existence of a greatest lower bound for any set follows from duality (Lemma ef{duality}) Recall the definition of $\widehat{X}$ for $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$ from Definition ef{hatconedef} and the definitions of $D_X$ and $D_e$ from Definition ef{mpccX}.  egin{lemma} Let $\{X_i\}_{i \in I}$ be a directed set in $\mathcal{L}_{n}$. Let $C_X =  igcup \widehat{X}_i$. Then $C_X$ is a convex cone with $X = C_X \cap \Phi_n^+ \in \mathcal{L}_{n}$ and $X =  igvee \{X_i\}_{i \in I}$. \end{lemma}  egin{proof} For each $X_i, i \in I$, we have $X_i = D_{X_i} \cap D_e \cap S^n$. Let $C_{X_i} = D_{X_i} \cap D_e $, then $C_{X_i}$ is a convex cone and by Lemma ef{hatcone}, $\widehat{X}_i = C_{X_i}$. To verify that $C_X$ is a convex cone, we need only verify that condition (3) of Definition ef{cones} holds, since conditions (1) and (2) are obvious. Given $u, v \in C_X$, we must have $\widehat{X}_i, \widehat{X}_j$ with $u \in \widehat{X}_i$ and $v \in \widehat{X}_j$ for some $i, j \in I$. Since $\{\widehat{X}_i\}_{i \in I}$ is a directed set, there exists $\widehat{X}_k, k \in I$, with $\widehat{X}_i \subseteq \widehat{X}_k$ and $\widehat{X}_i \subseteq \widehat{X}_k$. Therefore $u, v \in \widehat{X}_k$ and since $ \widehat{X}_k$ is a convex cone, we have $u + v \in \widehat{X}_k \subseteq C_X$. Thus $C_X$ is a convex cone. Let $X =  igcup_{i\in I} X_i$. We have $X = C_X \cap S^n$. We will show that there is a maximal pointed convex cone $D \subset \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ such that $X = D \cap \Phi^+_{n }$. For each $i \in I$, let $Y_i = \Phi^+_{n}  ackslash X_i$. Recall that $Y_i \in \mathcal{L}_{n }$. Hence $\widehat{Y}_i$ is a convex cone for each $i \in I$ and clearly $C_Y =  igcap_{i \in I} \hat{Y}_i$ is also a convex cone with $C_Y\cap C_X = \{0\}$ and $C_X \cup C_Y = D_e$. We let $D = C_X \cup (-C_Y)$. We have $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1} = C_X \cup (-C_Y) \cup C_Y \cup (-C_X) = D \cup (-D)$. It is clear that $D \cap (-D) = \{0\}$ and that $D\cup (-D) = D_e \cup (- D_e) = \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$. We show that $D$ is a maximal pointed convex cone. Conditions (1) and (2) of Definition ef{cones} are obvious. We need only show that if $u, v, \in D$, then $u + v$ is also in $D$. Since both $C_X$ and $(-C_Y)$ each have property (3), we can assume that $u \in C_X$ and $v \in (-C_Y)$. We can also assume that $u 
ot= 0$ and $v 
ot=0$, since otherwise the result is trivial. If $u + v 
ot\in C_X \cup (-C_Y)$, then we must have $u + v \in (-C_X) \cup C_Y$ and $u + v \in (-C_X)$ or $u + v \in C_Y$. If $u + v = -u_1$ for some $u_1 \in C_X$, we get $u + u_1 = -v \in C_X \cap (-C_Y) = \{0\}$, implying that $v = 0$ and giving us a contradiction. Similarly if $u + v = v_1$ where $v_1 \in C_Y$, we get a contradiction. Therefore $u + v \in C_X \cup (-C_Y) = D$ and $D$ is a maximal pointed convex set. Clearly $D\cap \Phi_n^+ = C_X \cap \Phi_n^+ = X$ and $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$. Since $X =  igcup_{i \in I}X_i$, we must have $X =  igvee \{X_i\}_{i \in I}$. \end{proof}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.2
nodes.statement:
For each $X_i, i \in I$, we have $X_i = D_{X_i} \cap D_e \cap S^n$. Let $C_{X_i} = D_{X_i} \cap D_e $, then $C_{X_i}$ is a convex cone and by Lemma ef{hatcone}, $\widehat{X}_i = C_{X_i}$. To verify that $C_X$ is a convex cone, we need only verify that condition (3) of Definition ef{cones} holds, since conditions (1) and (2) are obvious. Given $u, v \in C_X$, we must have $\widehat{X}_i, \widehat{X}_j$ with $u \in \widehat{X}_i$ and $v \in \widehat{X}_j$ for some $i, j \in I$. Since $\{\widehat{X}_i\}_{i \in I}$ is a directed set, there exists $\widehat{X}_k, k \in I$, with $\widehat{X}_i \subseteq \widehat{X}_k$ and $\widehat{X}_i \subseteq \widehat{X}_k$. Therefore $u, v \in \widehat{X}_k$ and since $ \widehat{X}_k$ is a convex cone, we have $u + v \in \widehat{X}_k \subseteq C_X$. Thus $C_X$ is a convex cone. Let $X =  igcup_{i\in I} X_i$. We have $X = C_X \cap S^n$. We will show that there is a maximal pointed convex cone $D \subset \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ such that $X = D \cap \Phi^+_{n }$. For each $i \in I$, let $Y_i = \Phi^+_{n}  ackslash X_i$. Recall that $Y_i \in \mathcal{L}_{n }$. Hence $\widehat{Y}_i$ is a convex cone for each $i \in I$ and clearly $C_Y =  igcap_{i \in I} \hat{Y}_i$ is also a convex cone with $C_Y\cap C_X = \{0\}$ and $C_X \cup C_Y = D_e$. We let $D = C_X \cup (-C_Y)$. We have $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1} = C_X \cup (-C_Y) \cup C_Y \cup (-C_X) = D \cup (-D)$. It is clear that $D \cap (-D) = \{0\}$ and that $D\cup (-D) = D_e \cup (- D_e) = \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$. We show that $D$ is a maximal pointed convex cone. Conditions (1) and (2) of Definition ef{cones} are obvious. We need only show that if $u, v, \in D$, then $u + v$ is also in $D$. Since both $C_X$ and $(-C_Y)$ each have property (3), we can assume that $u \in C_X$ and $v \in (-C_Y)$. We can also assume that $u 
ot= 0$ and $v 
ot=0$, since otherwise the result is trivial. If $u + v 
ot\in C_X \cup (-C_Y)$, then we must have $u + v \in (-C_X) \cup C_Y$ and $u + v \in (-C_X)$ or $u + v \in C_Y$. If $u + v = -u_1$ for some $u_1 \in C_X$, we get $u + u_1 = -v \in C_X \cap (-C_Y) = \{0\}$, implying that $v = 0$ and giving us a contradiction. Similarly if $u + v = v_1$ where $v_1 \in C_Y$, we get a contradiction. Therefore $u + v \in C_X \cup (-C_Y) = D$ and $D$ is a maximal pointed convex set. Clearly $D\cap \Phi_n^+ = C_X \cap \Phi_n^+ = X$ and $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$. Since $X =  igcup_{i \in I}X_i$, we must have $X =  igvee \{X_i\}_{i \in I}$.

nodes.name: X recovered from its cone
nodes.statement: Assertion (1) is trivial if $X = \emptyset$, so let us assume for now that $X \not= \emptyset$. We have $\widehat{X}$ is a union of rays, $\widehat{X} = \bigcup_{x \in X, x \not= 0} (x)$. Since each ray $(x)$ where $x \in X$ cuts the unit sphere exactly once at $x$, we have $X = \widehat{X} \cap S^n$.

nodes.name: uniqueness of the cone
nodes.statement: If C is a cone with $C \cap S^n = X$, then $\widehat{X} \subseteq C$, since the entire ray $(x)$ is in $C$ if $x \in X$. On the other hand, if $c \in C$, the ray $(c)$ cuts the sphere $S^n$ at $\frac{c}{||c||} \in X$. Therefore $(\frac{c}{||c||}) = (c) \in \widehat{X}$ and since $C$ is the union of such rays, we have $C \subseteq \widehat{X}$. This proves (1).
nodes.statement_short: Show $\widehat{X}=C$ by two inclusions of rays

nodes.name: part (2)
nodes.statement: We can now relax the assumption that $X \not= \emptyset$. It is easily seen that $\widehat{X} \cap \widehat{Y} = \widehat{X \cap Y}$. Assertion (2) follows from the observation that if $C$ is a cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$, then $C \cap S^n = \emptyset$ if and only if $C = \{0\}$.

nodes.name: easy inclusion
nodes.statement: Let $A \subset \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ be a convex cone. Since $ \bar{A} \cap S^n$ is closed and contains $A \cap S^{n}$, we have $\overline{A \cap S^{n} } \subseteq \bar{A} \cap S^n$.

nodes.name: approximating sequence
nodes.statement: On the other hand, if $x \in \bar{A} \cap S^n$, then $||x|| = 1$ and we have a sequence of points $\{x_i\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ in $A$ such that $\lim_{i \to \infty}x_i = x$. Since $A$ is convex we have the sequence of points $\{\frac{x_i}{||x_i||}\}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \in \bar{A} \cap S^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate $x$ by points of $A$ and normalize them

nodes.name: norm estimate
nodes.statement: Given any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $m$ such that $| ||x_i|| - 1 | = | ||x_i|| - ||x|| | \leq ||x_i - x|| < \epsilon $ for all $i \geq m$.

nodes.name: convergence
nodes.statement: Since $$||x - \frac{x_i}{||x_i||}|| \leq ||x - x_i|| + ||x_i - \frac{x_i}{||x_i||}|| = ||x - x_i|| + \frac{||x_i||(| \ ||x_i|| - 1|)}{||x_i||} \leq 2\epsilon$$ for $i \geq m$, we have that the sequence $\{\frac{x_i}{||x_i||}\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ converges to $x$ and $x \in \overline{A \cap S^{n} }$.

nodes.name: hyperplane in half space
nodes.statement: Suppose $u, v \in V$ with $H(u) \subseteq H_v = \{x \in V | <x, v> \leq 0 \}$. If $x \in H(u)$ with the property that $<x, v> \not= 0$, then $\{x,-x\} \in H(u)$ and either $<x, v> > 0$ or $<-x, v> > 0$ giving a contradiction. Hence $H(u) \subseteq H(v)$ and we have equality by comparing dimensions.
nodes.statement_short: Antipodal points force $H(u)\subseteq H(v)$, equal by dimension

nodes.name: nested half spaces
nodes.statement: If $H_u \subseteq H_v$, then $H(u) \subseteq H_v$ and therefore $H(u) = H(v)$. Now $V = <v> \bot H(v) = <u> \bot H(u) = <u> \bot H(v)$ and $u = cv$. Since $H_u \subseteq H_v$, $-u \in H_v$, hence $<-u, v> = <-cv, v> < 0$ and we have $c > 0$. Therefore $H_u = H_v$.

nodes.name: unit normal
nodes.statement: Let $v_1 \in H_v$ such that $H_{-v_1} = H_{v}$, then as above, $-v_1 = cv$ for some $c > 0$. If we assume $||v_1|| = 1$, then we must have $v_1 = \frac{-v}{||v||} $.

nodes.name: trivial direction
nodes.statement: Let $u, v \in V$. Clearly $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int} = \emptyset$ if $u = -cv$ for some $c > 0$ in $\Bbb{R}$.

nodes.name: assume disjoint
nodes.statement: Lets assume that $u \not= -cv, c > 0$. Suppose that $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int} = \emptyset$, then if $x \in H_u^{int}$ we must have $x \not\in H_v^{int}$ and $<x, v> \geq 0$ and $H_u^{int} \subseteq H_{-v}$.

nodes.name: contradiction
nodes.statement: Taking closures, we get $H_u \subseteq H_{-v}$ and by Lemma \ref{hyper} $H_u = H_{-v}$ and $u = -cv$ for some $c > 0$ giving us a contradiction.

nodes.name: setup
nodes.statement: Let $u$ and $v$ be as in the statement of the lemma and let $C = H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}$. Clearly the lemma is true if $u = cv$ for some $c > 0$. Therefore we will assume that $u \not= cv$ for any $c \in \Bbb{R}$ for the rest of the proof. In this case $H(u) \not= H(v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $u$ not a multiple of $v$

nodes.name: easy inclusion
nodes.statement: Since $\overline{H_u^{int}} = H_u$ and $\overline{H_v^{int}} = H_v$, we have $C \subseteq H_{u} \cap H_{v}$ and since $H_{u} \cap H_{v}$ is a closed set, we have $\bar{C} \subseteq H_{u} \cap H_{v}$.

nodes.name: reverse inclusion
nodes.statement: To verify the opposite inclusion, consider $x \in H_{u} \cap H_v$. If $x \in C$, then $x \in \bar{C}$. Therefore we need only consider points $x$ where $<x, u> = 0$ or $<x, v> = 0$ or both.

nodes.name: one boundary
nodes.statement: If $<x, u> = 0$ and $<x, v> > 0$, we have a sequence $\{x_i\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ in $H_{u}^{int}$ with $\lim_{i \to \infty} x_i = x$. Now since $x \in H_{v}^{int}$ which is an open set, there exists an $m$ for which $x_i \in H_{v}^{int}$ for all $i \geq m$. Therefore $x_i \in C$ for all $i \geq m$ and $x \in \bar{C}$. A similar argument shows that if $<x, v> = 0$ and $<x, u> < 0$, we have $x \in \bar{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Points on exactly one boundary hyperplane are limits of points of $C$

nodes.name: both boundaries
nodes.statement: Now if $<x, v> = 0$ and $<x, u> = 0$, then $x \in [H(u) \cap H(v)]$ which is a subspace of $H(v)$ of dimension $n - 2$ since $H(u) \not= H(v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Points on both hyperplanes lie in an $(n-2)$-dimensional subspace

nodes.name: remaining
nodes.statement: Let $H = [H(u) \cap H(v)]$. It remains to show that $H \subseteq \bar{C}$.

nodes.name: projection
nodes.statement: We consider $H$ as a hyperplane in $H(v)$. It is not difficult to see that if $y \in H(v)$, $<y, u> = < y, \pi(u)>$ where $\pi(u)$ is the orthogonal projection of $u$ onto the hyperplane $H(v)$. Therefore $$H = \{y \in H(v) | <y, \pi(u)> = 0 \} = H^{H(v)}(\pi(u))$$ as a hyperplane in $H(v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Express $H$ as a hyperplane in $H(v)$ via projection of $u$

nodes.name: conclude
nodes.statement: Now looking at the corresponding open half space in $H(v)$, we have $H_{\pi(u)}^{H(v){int}} = \{x \in H(v)| <x,\pi(u)> < 0\}$. By our reasoning above we know this is a subset of $\bar{C}$. Taking the closure within $H(v)$, we have $H^{H(v)}_{\pi(u)} = \overline{H_{\pi(u)}^{H(v)int} }\subseteq \bar{C}$ and $H = H^{H(v)}(\pi(u)) \subseteq \bar{C}$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Close the open half space within $H(v)$

nodes.name: Fenchel support
nodes.statement: According to Corollary 1 to Theorem 1 of Fenchel \cite{Fenchel}, a maximal pointed convex cone $D$ in $V$, has a support $H_{v}$, where $D \subseteq H_{v}$.

nodes.name: open half space inside D
nodes.statement: Now since $D \cup (-D) = V$ we have $H_v^{int} = \{x \in V | <x, v> < 0 \} \subseteq D$. Otherwise we would have $x \in (-D)$ with $<x, v> < 0$ and thus $<-x, v> > 0$ for $-x \in D$ giving us a contradiction.

nodes.name: closure equals support
nodes.statement: Thus we have $\overline{H_v^{int}} = H_{v} \subseteq \bar{D}$. On the other hand $\bar{D} \subseteq H_{v}$ since $D \subseteq H_{v}$, therefore $\bar{D} = H_v$.

nodes.name: uniqueness
nodes.statement: Suppose that $H_{u}$ is also a support. Then as above, we have $\bar{D} = H_u$ and hence $H_u = H_v$.

nodes.name: base case
nodes.statement: The result is obvious if $n = 1$, since the only maximal pointed convex cones of $\Bbb{R}e_1$ are $\Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}e_1$ and $\Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}(-e_1)$. We use induction on the dimension of $V$.

nodes.name: support
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$. From Theorem \ref{unique} we know that $D$ has a unique support $H_{v_{n }}$, where $D \subseteq H_{v_{n }}$ and $H_{v_n}^{int} \subseteq D$.

nodes.name: choose v_n
nodes.statement: From Lemma \ref{hyper} we know that we can choose a $v_n$ which is unique with the property that $-v_n \in D$, $||v_n|| = 1$ and $D \subseteq H_{v_{n }}$.

nodes.name: restricted cone
nodes.statement: Now consider the set $\widetilde{D} = D \cap H(v_{n })$. It is not difficult to see that $\widetilde{D}$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $H(v_{n })$.

nodes.name: inductive basis
nodes.statement: By induction, we get an orthonormal basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n - 1 }\}$ for $H(v_{n })$ such that $$\widetilde{D} = \{x \in H(v_{n }) | <x, v_m> < 0 \ \mbox{for} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | <x, v_m> \not= 0\}, 1\leq i \leq n -1 \} \cup \{0\}.$$

nodes.name: (1) implies (3)
nodes.statement: Now $D = \{x \in V | <x, v_{n }> < 0\} \cup \widetilde{D}$ and $$D = \{x \in V | <x, v_m> < 0 \ \mbox{for} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | <x, v_m> \not= 0\} , 1\leq i \leq n \} \cup \{0\}$$ where $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n\}$ is an orthonormal basis for $V$. This proves that (1) implies (3).

nodes.name: (2) implies (1)
nodes.statement: That (3) implies (2) is trivial. To show that (2) implies (1), let $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ be an ordered basis of $V$ and let $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ It is trivial to check that $D$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$. Therefore (2) implies (1).

nodes.name: injectivity setup
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$ with $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\} $$ where $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $V$. Suppose $\{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_n\}$ is another orthonormal basis of $V$ for which $$D = \{c_1u_1 + c_2u_2 + \dots + c_nu_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Two orthonormal bases giving the same cone

nodes.name: last vectors agree
nodes.statement: We have both $H_{u_n}$ and $H_{v_n}$ are supporting half spaces for $D$. Therefore, by Theorem \ref{unique} we have $H_{u_n} = H_{v_n}$ and since $||u_n|| = ||v_n|| = 1$, by Lemma \ref{hyper}, $u_n = v_n$.

nodes.name: remaining vectors
nodes.statement: Now $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1} \}$ and $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1} \}$ are ordered orthonormal bases of $H = H(u_n) = H(v_n)$ and $\widetilde{D} = D \cap H $ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $H$ with $$\widetilde{D} = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_{n- 1}v_{n-1} | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}$$ $$= \{c_1u_1 + c_2u_2 + \dots + c_{n- 1}u_{n-1} | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ Hence by induction, we have $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1} \}$ and $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1} \}$ are equal as ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and hence $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1}, u_n \}$ and\\ $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1}, v_n \}$ are equal as ordered orthonormal bases of $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction gives equality of the remaining vectors

nodes.name: bijection
nodes.statement: This shows that the map taking maximal pointed convex cones to ordered orthonormal bases given above is one to one. The map is onto since (3) implies (1).

nodes.name: simple transitivity
nodes.statement: Since the orthogonal group $O(V)$ acts simply transitively on the set of ordered orthonormal bases of $V$, and by linearity the action commutes with the above map from ordered orthonormal bases to maximal pointed convex cones in $V$, we have a simple transitive action of $O(V)$ on the set of maximal pointed convex cones in $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Transport simple transitivity from bases to cones

nodes.name: existence
nodes.statement: From its definition, we have that $D_{T_X}$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_{T_X} \cap \Phi_n^+ = T_X(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+ = X$.

nodes.name: second cone
nodes.statement: Suppose that $D$ is another maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = D \cap \Phi_n^+$. If $D_e = D_{-I_{\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}}}$, then $\Phi_n^+ = D_e \cap S^n$ and $X = D_X \cap D_e \cap S^n = D \cap D_e \cap S^n$.

nodes.name: equal parts
nodes.statement: Now $C_1 = D_X \cap D_e$ and $C_2 = D \cap D_e$ are both convex cones in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = C_1 \cap S^n = C_2 \cap S^n$. By Lemma \ref{hatcone}, $\hat{X} = C_1 = C_2$.

nodes.name: decompose and conclude
nodes.statement: Let $C'_1 = (D_e \backslash C_1) \cup \{0\} = D_e \cap (-D_X)$. Now $$[C_1 \cup (-C'_1) ] \cup [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = D_e \cup (-D_e) = \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$$ and $$[C_1 \cup (-C'_1) ] \cap [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = \{0\}$$ since $C_1 \cup (-C'_1) \subseteq D_X$ and $C'_1 \cup (-C_1) \subseteq -D_X$. Since $D_X \cap [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = \{0\}$, we can conclude that $D_X = C_1 \cup (-C'_1)$. Since $C'_1 = (D_e \backslash C_2) \cup \{0\} = D_e \cap (-D)$, we can similarly conclude that $D = C_1 \cup (-C'_1)$ and hence $D = D_X$.

nodes.name: cone of X
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$. There exists a maximal pointed convex cone $D$ in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ for which $X = D \cap \Phi_n^+$.

nodes.name: complement
nodes.statement: We have that $(-D)$ is also a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ and $(-D)\cap \Phi_n^+ = \Phi_n^+ \backslash X$. Hence $\Phi_n^+ \backslash X \in \mathcal{L}_n$. Since $\phi^2(X) = X$, it is easy to see that $\phi$ is a bijective map.
nodes.statement_short: $-D$ cuts out the complement; $\phi$ is an involution

nodes.name: order reversal
nodes.statement: Since $ \Phi_n^+ \backslash X \subseteq \Phi_n^+ \backslash Y$ if and only if $X \supseteq Y$, we have an isomorphism of posets $\phi: \mathcal{L}_n \to \mathcal{L}_n^{\delta}$.

nodes.name: restrict cone
nodes.statement: Given $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, we have a maximal pointed convex cone $D \subset \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ such that $X = D \cap \Phi_n^+$. Let $\widetilde{D} = D \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }$.

nodes.name: conclude
nodes.statement: It is not difficult to see that $\widetilde{D}$ is a maximal pointed convex cone of $\Bbb{R}^{n }$ and therefore $X \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } = D \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+ = \widetilde{D} \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+ \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Restricted cone is maximal, giving an element of $\mathcal{L}_{n-1}$

nodes.name: part (1)
nodes.statement: (1) follows from the fact that $X = T_X(\Phi^-_n) \cap \Phi^+_n$ and that $$ T_X(\Phi_n^-) = \{x \in S^n| x = \sum_{i = 1}^{n + 1}c_iT_X(e_i) \ \mbox{such that } \ c_m < 0 , \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i| c_i \not= 0\}\}.$$

nodes.name: part (3)
nodes.statement: Assertion (3) follows from (2) since, given (2), we have $$\bar{X}\cap S^{n -1} = [H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1}] \cap [H_{e} \cap S^{n - 1}] \cap [S^n \cap S^{n - 1}] = [H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1}] \cap S^{n - 1}.$$

nodes.name: remaining
nodes.statement: It remains to prove (2).

nodes.name: cone C
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be the convex cone $[H_{u_X}^{int} \cap H_{e}^{int}] \cup \{0\}$, the intersection of the two open half spaces with the zero vector attached. $C$ is non-empty by Lemma \ref{halfspaceintersect}.

nodes.name: sandwich
nodes.statement: Now $C \cap S^{n} \subset X \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n $ and hence $$ \overline{C \cap S^{n} } \subseteq \overline{X} \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n .$$

nodes.name: closures
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{cone} $$\overline{C} \cap S^{n} \subseteq \overline{X} \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n. $$ By Lemma \ref{closure}, $\bar{C} = H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}$.

nodes.name: conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore $\overline{X} = [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n$ and the result follows.

nodes.name: dimension options
nodes.statement: We have $ H(u_Y)\cap \Bbb{R}^{n } $ is a subspace of $\Bbb{R}^{n}$ of dimension $n$ or of dimension $n - 1$ .

nodes.name: dimension n-1
nodes.statement: Since we are assuming that $H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \not= \Bbb{R}^{n }$, it must be a subspace of dimension $n - 1$.

nodes.name: conclude
nodes.statement: Since $H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^n \subseteq H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^n$ it too must be a subspace of dimension $n - 1$ and hence must be all of $H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^n$.

nodes.name: restriction
nodes.statement: Since $T_Z$ is an isometry, with $T_Z(\Bbb{R}^n) = H(u_Z) = \Bbb{R}^n$, we have $T_Z|_{\Bbb{R}^n} = T'_Z \in O_n$.

nodes.name: conclude
nodes.statement: Now $||u_Z|| = 1$ and $<u_Z, x> = 0$ for all $x \in \Bbb{R}^n$. Hence $u_Z = \pm e_{n + 1}$ and $T_Z = T'_Z\bot \pm 1_{e_{n + 1}}$.

nodes.name: upper bound
nodes.statement: Let $Z \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with the property that $X\subseteq Z$ and $Y\subseteq Z$, where $Z = T_Z(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+$ for some $T_Z \in O_{n + 1}$. Let $u_Z = T_Z(e_{n + 1})$.
nodes.section: 5 The least upper bound of two elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$.

nodes.name: boundary traces
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{boundary} we have $\bar{Y}\cap \Bbb{R}^n = H_{u_Y} \cap S^{n - 1}$ and $\bar{Z}\cap \Bbb{R}^n = H_{u_Z} \cap S^{n - 1}$ and since $\bar{Y} \subseteq \bar{Z}$, we must have $H_{u_Y} \cap S^{n - 1} \subseteq H_{u_Z} \cap S^{n - 1}$.
nodes.section: 5 The least upper bound of two elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$.

nodes.name: assume proper
nodes.statement: If $H_{u_Z} \cap S^{n - 1} \not= S^{n - 1}$ then we must have that $H({u_Y}) \cap S^{n - 1} \subseteq H({u_Z}) \cap S^{n - 1}$, otherwise there exists $y \in H({u_Y}) \cap S^{n - 1}$ with $< y, u_Z> \not= 0$ and either $y$ or its antpodal point $-y$ is not in $ H_{u_Z} \cap S^{n - 1}$ giving a contradiction.
nodes.section: 5 The least upper bound of two elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$.

nodes.name: contradiction
nodes.statement: Therefore by Lemma \ref{equality} we have $H({u_Y}) \cap S^{n - 1} = H({u_Z}) \cap S^{n - 1}$. By a similar argument we have $H({u_X}) \cap S^{n - 1} = H({u_Z}) \cap S^{n - 1}$. However by assumption, $H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n} \not= H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n}$ and we have a contradiction.
nodes.section: 5 The least upper bound of two elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4.7 forces both traces equal, contradiction

nodes.name: full sphere
nodes.statement: Therefore, we must have $$S^{n - 1} = \bar{Z}\cap \Bbb{R}^n = H_{u_Z} \cap S^{n - 1} = H(u_Z) \cap S^{n - 1} \cup \{x \in S^{n - 1} | <x, u_Z> < 0\}.$$ If $x \in S^{n - 1}$ with $ <x, u_Z> < 0$, then $-x \in S^{n - 1}$ and $<-x , u_Z> > 0$. Therefore $\{x \in S^{n - 1} | <x, u_Z> < 0\} = \emptyset $ and $S^{n - 1} = H(u_Z) \cap S^{n - 1}$.
nodes.section: 5 The least upper bound of two elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$.

nodes.name: split T_Z
nodes.statement: Consequently $H(u_Z) = \Bbb{R}^n$ and $T_Z = T_Z' \bot \pm1_{e_{n + 1}}$ by Lemma \ref{Z}.

nodes.name: traces
nodes.statement: Let $X_1 = X \cap \Bbb{R}^n$ and $Y_1 = Y \cap \Bbb{R}^n$. Then by Theorem \ref{projection} we have $X_1 \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1} $ and $Y_1 \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$.

nodes.name: inductive join
nodes.statement: We proceed by induction. Let $Z_1 \in \mathcal{L}_{n -1}$ where $Z_1$ is the least upper bound of $\{X_1, Y_1\} $ in $ \mathcal{L}_{n -1}$. Then $Z_1 = D_{Z_1} \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+$ for a unique maximal pointed convex cone of $\Bbb{R}^n$.
nodes.section: 5 The least upper bound of two elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$.

nodes.name: construct Z
nodes.statement: Let $D_Z = D_{Z_1} \cup \{x \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1} | <x, e_{n + 1}> > 0\}$. It is not difficult to see that $D_Z$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_Z \cap \Bbb{R}^n = D_{Z_1}$. We let $Z = D_Z \cap \Phi_n^+ \in \mathcal{L}_n$.
nodes.section: 5 The least upper bound of two elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend $D_{Z_1}$ by the upper half space

nodes.name: upper bound
nodes.statement: Then $Z\cap S^{n - 1} = Z_1$ and therefore $$X = X_1 \cup [X \cap \{x \in S^n | <x, e_{n + 1}> > 0\}] \subseteq Z$$ and $$Y = Y_1 \cup [Y \cap \{x \in S^n | <x, e_{n + 1}> > 0\}] \subseteq Z.$$
nodes.section: 5 The least upper bound of two elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$.

nodes.name: other bound
nodes.statement: Now, if $W \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with the property that both $X$ and $Y$ are subsets of $W$, then Theorem \ref{conditions} tells us that $\{x \in S^n | <x, e_{n + 1}> > 0\} \subseteq W$.

nodes.name: least
nodes.statement: Since $W\cap S^{n - 1}$ contains both $X_1$ and $Y_1$ and, according to Theorem \ref{projection}, $W\cap S^{n - 1} \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$, we must have $Z_1 = Z\cap S^{n - 1} \subset W\cap S^{n - 1} \subseteq W$. Therefore $Z \subseteq W$ and $Z$ is the least upper bound of $\{X, Y\}$ in $\mathcal{L}_n$.

nodes.name: setup
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be as in the statement of the theorem with $\bar{X} \subseteq \bar{Y}$. Then $X = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+$ where $D_X$ and $D_Y$ are maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$. Suppose $Z = T_Z(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+ = D_Z\cap \Phi_n^+ \in \mathcal{L}_n$ is an upper bound for $\{X, Y\}$, where $T_Z \in O_{n + 1}$ and $D_Z$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$.
